source.title: A Continuous-Time Analysis of Distributed Stochastic Gradient

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; the paper identifies itself as an arXiv preprint.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports CIFAR-10 train and test performance for distributed SGD variants and compares their generalization, but does not test any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses large-batch generalization as prior work, but does not vary batch size. Its own CIFAR-10 experiments use minibatches of 128 and compare coupling and optimizer variants; these results bear on generalization but do not test a listed version. Table 1 reports test metrics for individual hyperparameter settings; only its aggregate conclusions are extracted here.
record.test_reason: The study measures CIFAR-10 performance under changes to distributed SGD coupling, agent count, initialization, and momentum. None tests V1–V8. In particular, changing agent count with local batches of 128 is not a controlled large-versus-small batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets. Adaptive optimizers are not compared, dropout is not ablated, and magnitude-aware sharpness is not measured. The discussion of large-batch generalization relies on prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that synchronization reduces stochastic gradient noise and loss smoothing; their CIFAR-10 experiments favor weaker coupling when convergence is retained and reveal an apparent regularizing benefit of EASGD, including without momentum in the single-agent setting. They propose investigating related higher-order optimization dynamics.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and evaluates distributed SGD variants and a single-agent EASGD variant; it does not use the random-label memorization experiments or interventions described in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization varies with coupling gain, number of agents, algorithm, and—in the single-agent comparison—learning rate and momentum parameter.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower coupling generally improves CIFAR-10 test performance provided the quorum variable still converges; insufficient coupling also performs poorly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distributed SGD generalization depends on coupling strength, with weaker coupling beneficial within the convergent regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing agent count improves performance in the tested regimes, while QSGD, SD-QSGD, and EASGD differ in generalization and stability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distributed SGD test performance and convergence depend on agent count and the dynamics used to couple agents.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-agent EASGD without momentum achieves the lowest minimum test error in all but one tested setting and the lowest minimum test loss in all but four.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feedback through an auxiliary parameter filter can improve CIFAR-10 generalization relative to the tested momentum SGD and EASGD configurations.

record.problems: The deep-network evidence is limited to one CIFAR-10 setup and a three-layer convolutional model. Most plotted values are not stated numerically in the text. Table 1 reports averages over three runs without error bars; its flattened presentation does not support reliable reconstruction of every individual cell.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports individual test-loss, test-error, and training-loss entries across learning-rate and momentum settings. Individual cell rows were omitted because the supplied table layout is flattened and the text gives aggregate conclusions; no other result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width needed to fit the training data.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers, tuning scope, and recovery through weight decay or switching.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce the penalty.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, including training-set size, dropout strength, and augmentation interactions.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparison with other measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Figures 11 and 12 additionally examine approximately matched synchronization and shared versus distinct initializations. These results also fit none of V1–V8, so they do not require missing claim-result rows. The paper's noise and smoothing analysis does not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization relationship.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels in the same architectures and recipes.
Width beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including the stated tuning and recovery conditions.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout ablations and the interaction with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: EASGD
rows.operation_detail: Varied coupling gain k while training on CIFAR-10 and measured classification error.

conditions.value: varied; text notes k = 0.01 and k = 0.02

rows.value: Text reports lower test errors for lower k values so long as convergence is obtained; k = 0.01 and k = 0.02 have too little synchronization for the quorum variable to represent a meaningful average.
rows.note: Values for individual plotted gains are figure-only; row records the text's qualitative comparison.
rows.check: The qualitative coupling result matches the text, but measures no listed version; partial is therefore inappropriate. EASGD is an optimizer, not the model. This is an algorithm-performance result that belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: QSGD
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of agents and measured test error while comparing QSGD with SD-QSGD.
rows.value: Text reports significant accuracy improvement as agent count increases; QSGD performs better for p = 32 and SD-QSGD does not converge for p = 64.
rows.note: Comparison includes SD-QSGD; the figure provides individual curves without textual numeric values.
rows.check: Agent-count scaling does not establish V5's batch-size effect. The row combines QSGD scaling with SD-QSGD comparisons and failure: SD-QSGD improves mildly over QSGD at p = 8 and 16, whereas QSGD performs better at p = 32 and 64. Both algorithms use momentum by default. This algorithm-performance comparison belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: EASGD
rows.operation_detail: Compared test performance with QSGD at a fixed coupling gain.
rows.value: EASGD generally drives test loss lower and test accuracy higher; for p = 16 it does not converge.
rows.note: The paper's text describes the comparison across experiments; individual plotted values are figure-only.
rows.check: The comparison matches the text but involves two non-adaptive distributed SGD variants, so it does not test V4. It also combines test loss and accuracy. EASGD is an optimizer; this method comparison belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: EASGD-WM
rows.operation_detail: Compared minimum test error with EASGD and SGD with momentum across learning rates and momentum parameters.
rows.value: EASGD-WM consistently achieves the lowest test error in all but one setting.
rows.uncertainty: Average over three independent runs; no error bars stated.
rows.note: Aggregate conclusion from settings reported separately in Table 1; the flattened table is not reconstructed into individual setting-level rows.
rows.check: The aggregate conclusion matches Table 1, but compares non-adaptive optimizers and tests no listed version. The value is the minimum over a trajectory averaged across three runs, not the average of per-run minima. The EASGD variants use k = 0.054 in this comparison. This method-performance summary belongs under fits_no_version.
